heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་གཉིས་པ།
translation: Regarding the second verse, "Homage to her whose face is like the autumn moon," the autumn moon is completely full, like a hundred full moons piled together, and her face is beautiful and extremely clear, resembling the light of a heap of fire. She is the one whose body is blazing with light that is spread out and radiating, like a gathering of thousands of stars; her body color is white, clear, and captivating, radiating white light. The hidden meaning is that the bodhicitta, like the autumn moon, is piled up without moving from the jewel at the crown of the head, and the fact that all the minor channels are completely filled is like the gathering of stars.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཞི་པ།
translation: Regarding the fourth verse, "Homage to the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgatas," the emanation of the wisdom of the *vidyā-mantra*—which possesses infinite benefits and acts to be completely victorious over all opposing forces—arises from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgata Vairocana. You, the virtuous one, having taken this as your own, enjoy it; you ensure the *vidyā-mantra* for countless sentient beings, and even the sons of the Victorious Ones, the lords of the ten grounds who have attained the ten *pāramitās* without remainder, rely upon and worship you with reverence. Regarding the profound meaning, the ground of joy in the order of arising and the order of reversal is as stated: "The glorious one who has thus gone, and who has thus gone again," which is the Tathāgata.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཞི་པ།
translation: By the dissolution of the collection of elements and winds into the *uṣṇīṣa*, one is completely victorious over infinite things to be abandoned, and by the transformation of the ten *pāramitās*—that is, the ten winds—the sons of the Victorious Ones, the Bodhisattvas, and the sense bases such as the eyes are also transformed into wisdom. Regarding the third verse, "Homage to her whose hand is beautifully adorned with a gold and blue water-born lotus," you, the goddess who holds in your hand a lotus that is blue and has a golden stem, are one who has attained mastery over the six pāramitās: generosity, diligence, austerity—which is ethical discipline—peace—which is wisdom—patience, and meditative concentration. Thus, the pāramitās are your very sphere of activity, and you, the goddess, are one who practices them. The hidden meaning is that the lotus, which is the place where the water-born flower resides, and the mudrā of the hand, which is the vajra—that is, the hands joined in equality—represent ethical discipline and austerity that do not waver, meditative concentration that is blissful, wisdom that pacifies conceptual thought through the realization of emptiness, diligence that is unceasing in that, patience that levels all happiness and suffering within that state, and generosity that has abandoned self-grasping; this is the teaching of the practice of mantra.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལྔ་པ།
translation: Regarding the fifth verse, "Homage to *tuttāra*," by the sound of the *mantra* of *tuttāra* and *hūṃ*, you pervade and fill all the abodes of the desire realm of this world, the sky—that is, the abodes of the form and formless realms—and by the term "directions," all other world-systems of the ten directions as well. You bring the seven worlds under your control, as if pressing them beneath your feet, and by the power of the *vidyā-mantra* that you have blessed, you possess the might to summon even great deities such as *Maheśvara* to serve as your servants; what need is there to mention others of lesser status? Regarding the "seven worlds," although there are many different ways of explaining them, such as the seven of the vessel, the seven of the sentient beings, or the seven of the combined vessel and sentient beings, here they refer to the seven powerful worlds: the worlds of the *nāgas*, *pretas*, *asuras*, humans, *vidyādharas*, *kiṃnaras*, and gods.

[1-5] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the fourth verse, "Homage to the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgatas," the emanation of the wisdom of the *vidyā-mantra*—which possesses infinite benefits and acts to be completely victorious over all opposing forces—arises from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Tathāgata Vairocana. You, the virtuous one, having taken this as your own, enjoy it; you ensure the *vidyā-mantra* for countless sentient beings, and even the sons of the Victorious Ones, the lords of the ten grounds who have attained the ten *pāramitās* without remainder, rely upon and worship you with reverence. Regarding the profound meaning, the ground of joy in the order of arising and the order of reversal is as stated: "The glorious one who has thus gone, and who has thus gone again," which is the Tathāgata.

By the dissolution of the collection of elements and winds into the *uṣṇīṣa*, one is completely victorious over infinite things to be abandoned, and by the transformation of the ten *pāramitās*—that is, the ten winds—the sons of the Victorious Ones, the Bodhisattvas, and the sense bases such as the eyes are also transformed into wisdom. This, along with the aforementioned "autumn moon" and so forth, constitutes the limbs of meditative concentration.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་ལྔ་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is that *tuttāra* is "torment," meaning to be tormented by the fire of *caṇḍālī*. The syllable *hūṃ* is the sound of the indestructible, which arises from *caṇḍālī*. "Desire" refers to the secret *cakra*, and "directions" refers to the inside of the *avadhūtī*, which is filled by that sound; the "sky" that is filled is that which is beyond expression. The "seven worlds" are the five *nāḍī-cakras* and the two *cakras* of fire and wind, making seven, which are filled by the *kuṇḍa* that melts from the blazing of *caṇḍālī*, and that very *kuṇḍa* is then summoned back, without remainder, from the secret *cakra* up to the crown of the head.

source: ཚིག་བཅད་དྲུག་པ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་སོགས་ལ། བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ནི་ལྷའི་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོའོ། །མེ་ལྷ་ནི་དྲང་སྲོང་གི་གཙོ་བོའོ། །ཚངས་པ་འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་བྱེད་པོར་འདོད་པའོ། །རླུང་ལྷ་ནི་འཇིག་རྟེན་གཟོའི་གནས་དང་བཀོད་པའི་ཁྱད་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །དྲག་པོ་དང་གཏོགས་འདོད་དང་། དྲང་སྲོང་ཉི་མའི་མདོག་དང་། ཕྱྭ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བྱེད་པོའམ་དབང་ཕྱུག་ཏུ་གྲགས་པ་སྣ་ཚོགས་པ་ནི། སྣ་ཚོགས་དབང་ཕྱུག་སྟེ། འཇིག་རྟེན་ན་ཆེས་ཆེ་བར་གྲགས་པ་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་། མཆོད་པའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་ཅིང་། འབྱུང་པོ་ནི་ཚོགས་ཀྱི་བདག་པོ་ལ་སོགས་པ་བགེགས་དང་ལོག་པར་འདྲེན་པ་རྣམས་སོ། །རོ་ལངས་ནི་རོ་ལངས་ཀྱི་ལས་བྱེད་པས་ལས་ཀྱི་མིང་བྱེད་པ་པོ་ལ་བཏགས་པ་སྟེ། ལྷའི་སྲིན་པོའི་རིགས་སྔགས་ཀྱི་མཐུ་གྲུབ་པ། རྫུ་འཕྲུལ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་འཇིགས་བྱེད་དགུ་ལ་སོགས་པའོ། །དྲི་ཟ་ནི་སྣ་ཚོགས་ཤིང་རྟ་ལ་སོགས་པ་རྣམས་དང་། གནོད་སྦྱིན་ནི་རྣམ་ཐོས་བུ་ལ་སོགས་པ་གཏེར་གྱི་བདག་པོ་རྣམས་དང་། མདངས་འཕྲོག་པའི་ལྷ་མ་སྲིན་རྣམས་ཏེ། འདུལ་བར་དཀའ་བའི་ཚོགས་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་། ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་མདུན་ནས་བསྟོད་པར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ་འགྲོ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ཀྱིས་བླ་མར་བསྔགས་སོ། །
translation: Regarding the sixth verse, "Homage to Indra, etc.," Indra is the king of the divine realms. Agni is the chief of the sages. Brahmā is considered the creator of the world. Vāyu is the one who establishes the specific locations and arrangements of the world. Rudra, Kāmadeva, the sage Sūrya, and various others who are renowned as creators or *īśvaras* are the "various *īśvaras*," and even those who are renowned as the greatest in the world have become objects of worship for you. *Bhūtas* are the hosts of *gaṇapati* and other such obstructors and misleading spirits. *Vetālas* are named after the work they perform, as they are those who perform the work of *vetālas*; they are of the class of *rākṣasas* who have attained the power of *mantra* and are the nine terrifying ones and others who possess great miraculous powers. *Gandharvas* are those such as the various *citraratha*, *yakṣas* are the lords of treasure such as Vaiśravaṇa, and the *piśācas* are the gods and demons who steal one's radiance; even those hosts who are difficult to tame offer praise before you, meaning that all beings praise you as their supreme guide.

The hidden meaning is that *tuttāra* is "torment," meaning to be tormented by the fire of *caṇḍālī*. The syllable *hūṃ* is the sound of the indestructible, which arises from *caṇḍālī*. "Desire" refers to the secret *cakra*, and "directions" refers to the inside of the *avadhūtī*, which is filled by that sound; the "sky" that is filled is that which is beyond expression. The "seven worlds" are the five *nāḍī-cakras* and the two *cakras* of fire and wind, making seven, which are filled by the *kuṇḍa* that melts from the blazing of *caṇḍālī*, and that very *kuṇḍa* is then summoned back, without remainder, from the secret *cakra* up to the crown of the head.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་དྲུག་པ།
source: སྦས་དོན་ནི་བརྒྱ་བྱིན་སོགས་ལྔ་ནི་འབྱུང་བ་ལྔ་སྟེ། བརྒྱ་བྱིན་ནི་ས། མེ་ལྷ་ནི་མེ། ཚངས་པ་ནི་ཆུ། རླུང་ལྷ་ནི་རླུང་། སྣ་ཚོགས་དབང་ཕྱུག་ནམ་མཁའ་འོ། །དེ་ལྟར་ཁམས་ལྔའི་རླུང་ཐིག་ལེར་ཐིམ་པ་ནི་མཆོད་པའོ། །འབྱུང་པོ་རྩ། རོ་ལངས་ཐིག་ལེ། དྲི་ཟ་རླུང་། གནོད་སྦྱིན་རྣམ་རྟོག་སྟེ། དེ་དག་ཀྱང་ཐིག་ལེར་ཐིམ་པ་ནི་མདུན་ནས་བསྟོད་པའོ། །འདིས་ནི་འཇིག་པའི་ཡན་ལག་བསྟན་ནོ། །
translation: The hidden meaning is that the five, beginning with Indra, are the five elements: Indra is earth, Agni is fire, Brahmā is water, Vāyu is wind, and the various *īśvaras* are space. In this way, the dissolution of the winds of the five elements into the *bindu* is the "worship." *Bhūtas* are the channels, *vetālas* are the *bindu*, *gandharvas* are the winds, and *yakṣas* are the conceptual thoughts; the dissolution of these into the *bindu* is the "praise from before." By this, the branch of dissolution is taught.

translation: Regarding the seventh verse, "Homage to *traṭ*," and so forth, the secret mantras of *traṭ* and *phaṭ*, and the like, are *vidyā-mantras* spoken by the Noble Tārā. Through the power of these wrathful practices, one becomes capable of performing various fierce activities; however, this is for the sake of subduing those who are difficult to tame for the benefit of others, and it is not a practice of causing harm. Through certain particulars of such *vidyā-mantras*, the power of the magical devices and mantras of opposing sorcerers is repelled and destroyed. Furthermore, by manifesting in a wrathful form and pressing down upon the malicious with feet positioned in the manner of right-bent and left-extended, she pacifies epidemics, contagious diseases, and the like. By displaying fire blazing and intensely flaming from her body, which is agitated by wrath, she causes spirits such as *yama* to scatter, and she performs a great protection for all beings.

translation: By the power of reciting the *rig-sngags* (mantra) of *oṃ tu-re* and so forth for the eighth verse, "Homage to Tu-re," and so on, Tārā herself manifests from the basic space of natural peace into the form of the Great Fearsome One. translation: Regarding the inner meaning of that: destroying the champions of Māra is the conduct of being completely victorious over all directions. The frown signifies that she has entered into the divine attire, which also signifies the attainment of the wisdom body. The hidden meaning is that *traṭ* signifies pacification, and *phaṭ* signifies splitting, which is to say, the destruction of conceptual thought. The magical devices of others, along with the winds of the twelve time-conjunctions of karma and kleshas, are blocked; the right channel, *ro-ma*, is drawn in, meaning its opening faces upward, and the left channel, *rkyang-ma*, is extended, meaning its opening faces downward. Pressing these two down completely with the foot of the *dbu-ma* (central channel) signifies that the winds of those two are blocked within the *dbu-ma*. From that, the fire of *gtum-mo* blazes, the water of the melting *haṃ* syllable is agitated, and again, it blazes intensely and melts greatly, and so forth; these are the limbs of *srog-rtsol* (breath control).

By this, she destroys the champions of Māra, that is, the military commanders, and by causing her lotus face to possess a frown, she slays the enemies who are hostile to the teachings, who harm many sentient beings, and who create obstacles for the practitioner; this means that they will be without the intention or the means to cause death or harm.

Regarding the inner meaning of that: destroying the champions of Māra is the conduct of being completely victorious over all directions. The frown signifies that she has entered into the divine attire, which also signifies the attainment of the wisdom body. The wisdom of non-dual bliss and emptiness is the "Great Fearsome One" because it causes those of inferior capacity to tremble. Through those two—the wisdom and the wisdom body—the enemies, namely the obscurations, are destroyed without exception, and by "Tu-re," meaning quickly, one traverses the higher paths and attains complete buddhahood. These are the twelve grounds, such as *kun-tu-'od* (the ground of universal light), which are the fruits of the limbs of meditative concentration.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་དགུ་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is that the Three Jewels represent the three of *khu* (semen), *rdul* (ovum), and *rlung* (wind); because they are gathered into one, the mudrā of the three fingers and so forth is fully bound at the *thig-le* (essence) of the central navel, which is the heart of each respective *rtsa-’khor-lo* (channel-wheel). By this, the wisdom body, formed from the light rays of *gtum-mo* (inner heat), pervades all directions, which is the meaning of attaining it; through the power of holding [this], mindfulness arises.

translation: Regarding the eleventh verse, "Homage to her who has the power to summon all the hosts of local guardians," and so forth: she is the one who possesses the power to summon and bring under her control all the hosts of kings who protect the earth, the earth goddesses, and so forth, as well as the subterranean nāgas, asuras, vidyādharas, and hosts of ḍākinīs, by means of her vidyā-mantra. translation: The hidden meaning is that by the sound of "local guardians" and "lords of the subterranean," one summons the essence of the elements in the manner of relying upon them from the *uṣṇīṣa* down to the *maṇi*; and by the sound of "vibrating frown" and *hūṃ*, the essence of the "hare-marked" (the moon) is the "frown," which, passing through the *tilaka* at the center of the eyebrows and becoming stable up to the *uṣṇīṣa*, is the liberation from poverty for the sake of accomplishing meditative absorptions such as the "sky-treasury." This is the characteristic of the limb of meditative absorption, which is the manner of blocking the movement of the white and red [elements] in the upper and lower [channels].

Work: ཏཱ་ར་ན་ཐའི་སྒྲོལ་མ་ཉེར་གཅིག་ལ་བསྟོད་པའི་རྣམ་བཤད། (author: Tāranātha). A canonical Tibetan text; the blocks below are being translated one at a time, in order.

Preceding blocks of this same document and their translations — match this terminology, register and line shape:

[1-21] source:
ཚིགས་བཅད་བཅུ་གཉིས་པ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཟླ་བའི་སོགས་ལ། ཟླ་བའི་དུམ་བུ་ནི་ཟླ་བ་ཕྱེད་པས་དབུ་བརྒྱན་ལ་བརྒྱན་པ་ལས་དང་། གཞན་ཡང་རྒྱན་གྱིས་བརྒྱན་པ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལས་འོད་ཟེར་རབ་ཏུ་འབར་བས། ཕྱུག་བདག་ཆེན་པོ་བྱེ་བ་ཕྲག་བརྒྱའི་དྲེགས་པ་འཇོམས་པ་མོ། ལན་འགའ་དཀའ་ཐུབ་ཅན་གྱི་སྐུར་བསྟན་ནས། རལ་པའི་ཐོར་ཚུགས་འཆར་བའི་ཁྲོད་ན་དེ་བཞིན་གཤེགས་པ་འོད་དཔག་ཏུ་མེད་པ་བཞུགས་ཤིང་གནས་པའི་སྐུ་ལས། རྟག་ཏུ་རྒྱུན་མི་འཆད་པར་ཤིན་ཏུ་འོད་རབ་བྱེད་མ་སྟེ། འོད་ཀྱི་སྣང་བས་གསལ་བར་བྱེད་པའོ། །
[1-21] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the twelfth verse, "Homage to her whose head is adorned with a crescent moon," and so forth: the "crescent moon" refers to her being adorned with a half-moon as a crown ornament, and because rays of light blaze intensely from all her other ornaments as well, she is the one who subdues the arrogance of the great lords of wealth, the hundreds of millions. By manifesting at times in the form of an ascetic, she is the one who, from the midst of her rising matted locks, where Amitābha resides and dwells, constantly and without interruption radiates a most intense light, illuminating everything with the radiance of that light.

[1-22] source:
སྦས་དོན་ནི། གོང་སྔ་མའི་འཕྲོས་དེ་ཉིད་ལ་སྦྱར་ཏེ། ཟླ་བའི་དུམ་བུའི་དབུ་རྒྱན་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་སྤྱི་བོར་བརྟན་པའོ། །རལ་པའི་ཁྲོད་གནས་ནི་གྲིབ་མའི་ཚུལ་དུ་སྤྱི་བོར་བརྟན་པ། འོད་དཔག་མེད་ནི་དམར་ཆའི་དངས་མ། དེ་གཉིས་དཀར་ལ་འོད་ཟེར་རབ་ཏུ་འཕྲོ་པ་ནི། དཀར་དམར་དེ་རྣམས་སྟོང་གཟུགས་ཕྱག་རྒྱ་ཆེན་པོའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་གྱི་འཁོར་ལོ་མཐའ་ཡས་པར་གྱུར་པའོ། །
[1-22] translation already produced for this document:
The hidden meaning is to be applied to the preceding context: the "crescent moon" crown ornament is the bodhicitta stabilized at the crown of the head. "Residing amidst the matted locks" is the stabilization at the crown in the manner of a shadow. "Amitābha" is the quintessence of the red element. That these two, the white and the red, radiate intense light means that those white and red elements have become the infinite wheels of the maṇḍala of the great seal of empty form.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་གསུམ་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is: the *caṇḍālī* wisdom fire is like the blazing fire at the end of time. The flow that arises, pervading the entire body and all appearances, is the "right leg extended and left bent," meaning the right and left *ro* and *kyang* channels, or the upper and lower life-sustaining and downward-moving winds, which surround on all sides. This refers to the various manifestations of her play, such as the manner in which the five elements dissolve, each occurring within their respective energy centers. By "joy," it is meant that because the winds have become the drop of bliss, she destroys the enemy armies of the māras and the afflictions.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་བཞི་པ།
translation: Regarding the fourteenth verse, "Homage to her who strikes the surface of the earth," and so forth: she strikes the surface of the great earth, which includes Mount Meru and the continents, with the palm of her hand. By striking it with her feet and assuming a wrathful, frowning countenance, she uses the power of her wrath to proclaim the terrifying sound of "Hūṃ" from her nose, thereby shattering all the malicious nāgas, asuras, rākṣasas, and pretas dwelling in the seven levels beneath the earth, causing them to be scattered into pieces.

source: དེ་ལས་འོག་བདུན་ནི། ས་གཞི་ཆེན་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་ལ། འོག་ཏུ་ཐོག་ཕུགས་རིམ་པ་བདུན་བཞིན་དུ་མི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི་ཡུལ་ཆེན་པོ་དག་གནས་པའོ། །ཁ་ཅིག་ནི་རི་རབ་ཀྱི་རྩེ་མོའི་ཁོངས་སེང་ནས་ཐུར་དུ་གཞལ་བ་ཡིན་ཟེར་ཡང་མི་ལེགས་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ཡང་གཞི་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་གཞི་དང་། གཞི་མེད་པ་དང་། གཞི་ཉིད་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་གཞི་དང་། གཞི་བཟང་པོ་དང་། དག་པའི་གཞི་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ས་འོག་གི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་སོ། །
translation: As for the seven levels beneath that: beneath this very great earth, there exist seven successive levels of great realms of non-human beings. Although some say that these are measured downwards from the hollow space at the summit of Mount Meru, this does not appear to be correct. They are called the Basis, the Superior Basis, the Baseless, the Basis Itself, the Basis of Essence, the Good Basis, and the Pure Basis. These are the great worlds beneath the earth.

The hidden meaning is: the *caṇḍālī* wisdom fire is like the blazing fire at the end of time. The flow that arises, pervading the entire body and all appearances, is the "right leg extended and left bent," meaning the right and left *ro* and *kyang* channels, or the upper and lower life-sustaining and downward-moving winds, which surround on all sides. This refers to the various manifestations of her play, such as the manner in which the five elements dissolve, each occurring within their respective energy centers. By "joy," it is meant that because the winds have become the drop of bliss, she destroys the enemy armies of the māras and the afflictions.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་བཞི་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is as follows: the surface of the earth is the mandala of the navel, which is struck by the feet of the goddess—who is the definitive meaning—and pressed by her hands of flame, through the fire of *caṇḍālī* wisdom. These seven levels beneath the earth are the seven coils of the *caṇḍālī* fire, which resembles a coiled serpent, residing at the lower end of the *avadhūtī*. When the *bodhicitta* of the blazing *caṇḍālī* arrives there, the torment of the fire is completely pacified, and the knots of the channels are shattered and destroyed.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅོ་ལྔ་པ།
source: ཚིགས་བཅད་བཅོ་ལྔ་པ་ཕྱག་འཚལ་བདེ་མ་སོགས་ལ། བཅོམ་ལྡན་འདས་མ་ཉིད་རྟག་ཏུ་བདེ་བ་དང་། དགེ་མ་དང་། ཞི་བའི་ངང་ཚུལ་ཅན་མ། མྱ་ངན་ལས་འདས་པ་མཆོག་ཏུ་ཞི་བ། འགོག་བདེན་གྱི་དབྱིངས་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་པས་ཞི་བའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ཅན་མ་སྟེ། དེའི་ཕྱིར་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམས་ལ། ཚེ་འདིའི་བདེ་བ་དང་། ཕ་རོལ་གྱི་དོན་དུ་དགེ་བ་བསྐྱེད་པར་མཛད་པ་མ། སྐལ་པ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ལ། ཞི་བའི་ལམ་སྟོན་པར་མཛད་ཅིང་། འབྲས་བུ་མི་གནས་པའི་མྱང་འདས་ཞི་བ་དམ་པའི་སྤྱོད་ཡུལ་ལ་འགོད་པར་མཛད་པ་སྟེ། གཞན་ཡང་ལྷ་མོ་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་གསུངས་པའི་རིག་སྔགས་སྭཱ་ཧཱ་དང་ཨོཾ་དང་ཡང་དག་པར་ལྡན་བདག་བཟླས་པས། སྡིག་པ་ཆེན་པོ་དང་དེའི་འབྲས་བུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱང་འཇོམས་པར་མཛད་པ་ཉིད་དོ། །འདིས་ཞི་བའི་ལས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་བསྒྱུར་བའི་སྔགས་སྭཱ་ཧཱ་ར་བཤད་ཅིང་། གོང་དུ་ཟློག་པ་ལ་ཏྲཊ་དང་། བསད་པ་ལ་ཕཊ་དུ་གསུངས་པས། ལས་གཞན་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྔགས་ཀྱི་མཐའ་བསྒྱུར་བ་ཡང་ཞོར་ལ་འཕངས་པ་ཡིན་ནོ། །
translation: Regarding the fifteenth verse, "Homage to the Blissful, Virtuous, and Peaceful One," and so forth: the Blessed One herself is always blissful, virtuous, and of a peaceful nature. Because she is in the state of nirvāṇa, which is supreme peace, and remains in equipoise within the expanse of the truth of cessation, she is one whose sphere of experience is peace. Therefore, she generates the happiness of this life for sentient beings, as well as virtue for the sake of the hereafter. For those who are fortunate, she teaches the path of peace and establishes them in the sphere of experience of the supreme peace of nirvāṇa, which is the fruit of non-abiding. Furthermore, by reciting the *vidyā-mantra* spoken by the goddess herself, which is perfectly endowed with *svāhā* and *oṃ*, she also destroys great negativity and the great suffering that is its fruit. By this, the *svāhā* that concludes the mantra for the activity of pacification is explained; and since it was stated above that *traṭ* is for repelling and *phaṭ* is for killing, the conclusion of the mantras for other activities is also incidentally indicated.

དེ་ལས་འོག་བདུན་ནི། ས་གཞི་ཆེན་པོ་འདི་ཉིད་ལ། འོག་ཏུ་ཐོག་ཕུགས་རིམ་པ་བདུན་བཞིན་དུ་མི་མ་ཡིན་གྱི་ཡུལ་ཆེན་པོ་དག་གནས་པའོ། །ཁ་ཅིག་ནི་རི་རབ་ཀྱི་རྩེ་མོའི་ཁོངས་སེང་ནས་ཐུར་དུ་གཞལ་བ་ཡིན་ཟེར་ཡང་མི་ལེགས་པར་མངོན་ནོ། །དེ་ཡང་གཞི་དང་། ལྷག་པའི་གཞི་དང་། གཞི་མེད་པ་དང་། གཞི་ཉིད་དང་བཅུད་ཀྱི་གཞི་དང་། གཞི་བཟང་པོ་དང་། དག་པའི་གཞི་ཞེས་བྱའོ། །ས་འོག་གི་འཇིག་རྟེན་ཆེན་པོ་རྣམས་སོ། །
[1-26] translation already produced for this document:
As for the seven levels beneath that: beneath this very great earth, there exist seven successive levels of great realms of non-human beings. Although some say that these are measured downwards from the hollow space at the summit of Mount Meru, this does not appear to be correct. They are called the Basis, the Superior Basis, the Baseless, the Basis Itself, the Basis of Essence, the Good Basis, and the Pure Basis. These are the great worlds beneath the earth.

[1-27] source:
སྦས་དོན་ནི། ས་གཞིའི་ངོས་ནི་ལྟེ་བའི་དཀྱིལ་འཁོར་ཏེ། དེ་ལ་གཏུམ་མོ་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་མེ་ངེས་པའི་དོན་གྱི་ལྷ་མོའི་ཞབས་ཀྱིས་བརྡུངས་པ་དང་མེ་ལྕེའི་ཕྱག་གིས་བསྣུན་པའོ། །དེ་ཡང་ས་འོག་བདུན་ཏེ། དབུ་མའི་མས་སྣ་ན་ཚངས་པའི་མེ་སྤུལ་ལྟར་འཁིལ་བ་ལན་བདུན་པ། རབ་ཏུ་འབར་བ་གནས་པ་དེར། གཏུམ་མོ་འབར་བའི་བྱང་ཆུབ་ཀྱི་སེམས་འོངས་བ་ན་མེའི་གདུང་བ་རབ་ཏུ་ཞི་བ་དང་། དེའི་རྩ་མདུད་རྣམས་འགེམས་ཤིང་འཇིགས་པའོ། །
[1-27] translation already produced for this document:
The hidden meaning is as follows: the surface of the earth is the mandala of the navel, which is struck by the feet of the goddess—who is the definitive meaning—and pressed by her hands of flame, through the fire of *caṇḍālī* wisdom. These seven levels beneath the earth are the seven coils of the *caṇḍālī* fire, which resembles a coiled serpent, residing at the lower end of the *avadhūtī*. When the *bodhicitta* of the blazing *caṇḍālī* arrives there, the torment of the fire is completely pacified, and the knots of the channels are shattered and destroyed.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅོ་ལྔ་པ།
translation: The ultimate definitive meaning of this is: the Blissful One is the wisdom of discernment; the Virtuous One is the mirror-like wisdom; the Peaceful One is the wisdom of equality; the one who is peaceful in nirvāṇa is the wisdom of the expanse of phenomena; and the one who destroys great negativity is the all-accomplishing wisdom. Because the indestructible sound of the speech, represented by the *vidyā-mantra* *oṃ* and *svāhā*, arises boundlessly, she performs the benefit of sentient beings, such as pacifying negativity, which is to say that this is applied to the result.

[1-28] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the fifteenth verse, "Homage to the Blissful, Virtuous, and Peaceful One," and so forth: the Blessed One herself is always blissful, virtuous, and of a peaceful nature. Because she is in the state of nirvāṇa, which is supreme peace, and remains in equipoise within the expanse of the truth of cessation, she is one whose sphere of experience is peace. Therefore, she generates the happiness of this life for sentient beings, as well as virtue for the sake of the hereafter. For those who are fortunate, she teaches the path of peace and establishes them in the sphere of experience of the supreme peace of nirvāṇa, which is the fruit of non-abiding. Furthermore, by reciting the *vidyā-mantra* spoken by the goddess herself, which is perfectly endowed with *svāhā* and *oṃ*, she also destroys great negativity and the great suffering that is its fruit. By this, the *svāhā* that concludes the mantra for the activity of pacification is explained; and since it was stated above that *traṭ* is for repelling and *phaṭ* is for killing, the conclusion of the mantras for other activities is also incidentally indicated.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་པ།
translation: Regarding the sixteenth verse, "Homage to Her who is surrounded by those of intense joy and utterly shatters the bodies of enemies," those who are *vidyādhara* adepts, bodhisattvas, and those possessing the samādhi and the mind of intense joy surround Her. She utterly shatters—that is, disperses—the bodies of enemies, such as the sinful lord of the Paranirmitavaśavartin realm, who are harmful to sentient beings. You are the Goddess who has emerged from the arrangement of the ten-syllable speech, the mantra. You are the Illuminator, the one whose body blazes with light, who has emerged from the *vidyā-mantra*—the *vidyā*—of the syllable HŪṂ. By this, the wrathful Tārā is shown to have the seed syllable HŪṂ and the ten-syllable mantra of approach.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་དྲུག་པ།
translation: The definitive meaning is: through the light rays of the empty-form Mahāmudrā, one is surrounded by intense joy, which is the unchanging bliss; by this, one destroys the enemy, which is the body of impure appearance. This refers to the branch of meditative concentration. The ten syllables are the ten signs obtained from the cessation of the parts of the ten mandalas of the right and left [channels]. Furthermore, the syllables represent the winds, and the etymological meaning of the syllable, *akṣara*, is "unchanging," meaning the ten appearances of the unchanging expanse of phenomena, or the ten parts of unchanging bliss that arise from perceiving them.

[1-31] translation already produced for this document:
The definitive meaning is: through the light rays of the empty-form Mahāmudrā, one is surrounded by intense joy, which is the unchanging bliss; by this, one destroys the enemy, which is the body of impure appearance. This refers to the branch of meditative concentration. The ten syllables are the ten signs obtained from the cessation of the parts of the ten mandalas of the right and left [channels]. Furthermore, the syllables represent the winds, and the etymological meaning of the syllable, *akṣara*, is "unchanging," meaning the ten appearances of the unchanging expanse of phenomena, or the ten parts of unchanging bliss that arise from perceiving them.

[1-32] source:
རིག་པ་ཧཱུྃ་གི་བརྡས་ནི། ཧཱུྃ་ཆ་ལྔ་པས་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལྔ་མཚོན་ཏེ་ཡེ་ཤེས་ལྔའི་རང་བཞིན་གྱི་ཐིག་ལེ་ཁམས་གསུམ་གྱི་གཟུགས་བརྙན་དང་བཅས་པའོ། །དེ་ཡང་རྟགས་བཅུ་པོ་དེ་དག་གི་ཆོས་སུ་འཇོག་སྟེ་རླུང་དབུ་མར་བཀང་བ་ལས་བྱུང་བས་སོ། །དེ་ལ་མཉམ་པར་འཇོག་པ་ནི་དོན་དམ་པའི་རིག་སྔགས་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ་སྒྲོན་མ་ནི་སྟོང་གཟུགས་ཀྱི་གསལ་སྣང་ངོ། འདི་ནི་སོ་སོར་སྡུད་པའི་རྣལ་འབྱོར་རོ། །
[1-32] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the sign of the *vidyā* HŪṂ: the five-part HŪṂ represents the five wisdoms, which are the *bindus* of the nature of the five wisdoms, together with the reflections of the three realms. These are established as the phenomena of those ten signs because they arise from filling the central channel with wind. Remaining in equipoise regarding this is the supreme *vidyā-mantra* of ultimate reality, and the "Illuminator" is the clear appearance of empty form. This is the yoga of withdrawal.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་བདུན་པ།
translation: The phrase "the form of HŪṂ" refers to *hūṃ-kāra*, the syllable HŪṂ. The phrase "in the three worlds" uses the seventh case to indicate the object of the second case, meaning that the action of shaking is applied to the three worlds. If the three worlds are shaken, one might ask, what is the point of mentioning Mount Meru and the others? Although the three worlds in general are shaken, it is possible that those specific places where powerful deities reside might not be shaken; therefore, they are mentioned to signify the great power of the Āryā herself.

[1-34] translation already produced for this document:
If we follow the reading "Vindhya" (the Piercer) that appears in most Tibetan editions, then it is the king of mountains, the Piercer. However, in those versions of this text where the Sanskrit is visible, it appears as Kailāśa; if that is the case, it accords with the reading "Snowy Mountain." Because various editions appear, it is difficult to fix upon one, so it should be understood in a way that both are not contradictory.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་བཅུ་བདུན་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is as follows: Mount Meru is the bone of Brahmā; the other two mountains are Yid-bzang-ma and Dung-can-ma; "shaking" means being completely filled with the bodhicitta; the "three worlds" are the six channels, divided into three upper and three lower. Regarding the sign of HŪṂ: it is the *avadhūtī*, the mind-vajra channel, which is the seed of all channels, and the power is dissolved therein.

Regarding the nineteenth verse, "Homage to the queen of the hosts of gods," the "hosts of gods" refers to the six classes of gods of the desire realm. Likewise, "king" refers to those who exercise power in this world, such as universal monarchs and others. The mountain deities, tree deities, and lake goddesses, and so forth, who bring benefit or harm in the world, are specific types of gods; these, along with the powerful kinnaras, rely upon your lotus feet with devotion. By the practitioner who is completely bound by the armor of the mantra and mudrā blessed by you, O Goddess, the majesty of body, speech, and mind dispels all disharmony, such as the disputes of others and bad dreams. Here, "armor" means protection.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཉི་ཤུ་པ།
translation: Regarding the twentieth verse, "Homage to the one whose two eyes...", when she gazes upon all beings with a vision that is extremely brilliant, like the rays of light fully expanded from the sun and moon, she establishes all beings who are suffering, such as those in the lower realms, in happiness. By reciting the *hara* mantra twice, along with the *tuttāra* mantra, she dispels even the most violent and incurable epidemic diseases. In terms of the immediate context, the ten-syllable mantra is taught to pacify epidemic diseases, halt plagues, and protect against contagious illnesses; however, the primary meaning is that by reciting the ten syllables, one pacifies all defilements, which are like violent epidemic diseases.

translation: In this context, the two eyes are likened to the sun and moon because the light of the right eye terrifies those who cause harm and burns away sins and suffering, thus it is light like the sun; and because the rays of the left eye bestow life, enjoyment, and happiness, it is the light of the moon that radiates nectar. The phrase "uttering Tāra twice" identifies the two *tāre* and *tuttāre* syllables, which is the very same ten-syllable speech mentioned previously. Therefore, it is the complete *oṃ tāre tuttāre ture svāhā*, which is the mantra for all three—the peaceful, increasing, and wrathful—practices of Tārā.

heading: ཕྱག་འཚལ་ཉི་ཤུ་པ།
translation: The hidden meaning is that the sun and moon symbols represent the two internal *khu-rdul* (semen and ovum). The eyes that are completely filled by these are the two mantras at the top and bottom of the *avadhūtī*, and because primordial wisdom arises from them, they are "brilliantly radiant." The two *hara* syllables mean "to liberate," signifying liberation from the two extremes of existence and quiescence through bliss and emptiness. *Tuttāre* means "torment," which is asceticism; by pressing the sun downward and fixing the moon at the crown, this unchanging asceticism dispels the epidemic disease of the shifting *bindu*.

translation: Regarding the twenty-first verse, "Homage to her who is perfectly endowed with the power of peace," and so forth, there are four aspects: the meaning of the syllables, the general meaning, the hidden meaning, and the ultimate meaning. The first is that because the mind of the trainee is perfectly established in the three suchnesses—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—through their power, all obscurations are abandoned and one is established in peace; thus, she is the one perfectly endowed with the power to ripen and liberate the trainee.

heading: གསུམ་པ་སྦས་དོན།
translation: The third is the hidden meaning: the three suchnesses are appearance, increase, and near-attainment. Once the arrangement of these has dawned in sequence, it proceeds to the pacification—that is, the momentary pacification of all—which is the empty clear light. By destroying the "spirits" (the channels), the "zombies" (the bindus), and the "yakṣas" (the conceptual thoughts) within the expanse of clear light, one swiftly arises in the supreme form of the deity.

"Spirits" refers to the eighteen types of spirits, such as the *nam-gu* spirits. "Zombies" refers to the work of zombies, that is, malevolent mantras such as those for casting and sending. "Yakṣas" refers to the harm caused by those who steal one's vitality. All such harm is destroyed by the three gates of liberation, and it is also destroyed through the power of the mantra "supreme *ture*." Alternatively, *ture* means "the swift one," signifying that you, the supreme goddess, swiftly destroy all harm. Since it can also be interpreted in this way, it is correct to emend it to "the supreme mother who swiftly destroys."

translation: The fourth is the ultimate: these three—the vajra of body, speech, and mind—are established from the beginning as the nature of all phenomena. heading: རྩ་བའི་སྔགས་ཀྱི་དོན།
source: དེ་ལ་རྩ་བའི་སྔགས་ཀྱི་དོན་ནི། ཨོཾ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་མཆོག་གི་ཚངས་པ། ཆོས་ཀྱི་དབྱིངས་ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ། ཡོན་ཏན་མཐའ་དག་གི་ནོར་བུ་འཛིན་པ། བདེ་བར་གཤེགས་པའི་སྙིང་པོ་ཆོས་ཀྱི་མཆོག་གོ། །ཆོས་ཀྱི་སྐུ་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ནི་ཏཱ་རེ། གདོད་མའི་ཆོས་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་སྐུ་ནི་ཏུཏྟཱ་རེ། བརྗོད་དུ་མེད་པའི་ཆོས་ལས་བྱུང་བ་སྙིང་རྗེ་ཆེན་པོ་ནི་ཏུ་རེ་སྟེ་སྤྲུལ་པ་དང་མཛད་པའོ། །སྭཱ་ནི་རང་བྱིན་གྱིས་བརླབས་པ། ཧཱ་ནི་ཧ་ལས་ཨཱ་ར་ལི་སྟེ། ཨེ་མ་ཧོ་རོལ་པ་སྟེ། སྒྱུ་མ་ལྟ་བུའི་སྐུ་དང་ཞིང་ཁམས་དང་མཛད་པ་མཐའ་ཡས་པའོ། །དོན་དེ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་སྒོ་ནས་བསྟོད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རྩ་བའི་སྔགས་ཀྱིས་བསྟོད་པའོ། །
translation: Regarding the meaning of the root mantra: "Oṃ" is the supreme purity, the dharmadhātu, the dharmakāya, the holder of the jewel of all qualities, and the supreme dharma, the essence of the Sugatas. Tāre is the primordial wisdom arising from the dharmakāya; Tuttāre is the body arising from the primordial dharma; Ture is the great compassion arising from the ineffable dharma, representing the emanation and the activity. Svā is self-blessing; Hā is Ārali derived from Ha, meaning "Emaho," the display, which is the infinite body, pure realm, and activity that are like an illusion. Because it praises by means of these meanings, it is a praise by the root mantra.

Tāre is the primordial wisdom arising from the dharmakāya; Tuttāre is the body arising from the primordial dharma; Ture is the great compassion arising from the ineffable dharma, representing the emanation and the activity. Svā is self-blessing; Hā is Ārali derived from Ha, meaning "Emaho," the display, which is the infinite body, pure realm, and activity that are like an illusion. Because it praises by means of these meanings, it is a praise by the root mantra.

heading: ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: Having risen at dusk and at dawn—that is, having performed the act of rising—and with prostration and offering preceding it, one should keep the qualities of the Āryā in mind. The benefits of this are that she grants all fearlessness; she protects from all fears, such as the eight great fears and the sixteen fears, and she bestows the perfect mastery of the state of fearlessness. Regarding the phrase "recites with diligence" (rab dang brjod cing), since the Sanskrit word "va" is present, it is correct to translate it as "recites with effort." Therefore, if any intelligent person, through the six sessions from dusk onwards, remains reverent toward the Goddess and, by way of remembering her qualities, recites this praise with effort, these benefits will be present; this is how it should be understood throughout the entire preceding and following text.

heading: ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: "Sin" refers to the fruits of sin; all previously existing illnesses, malevolent spirits, misfortunes, and unfortunate destinies are thoroughly pacified, and those that would have arisen again are averted. Likewise, even if one is a person whose karma makes birth in the lower realms certain due to the power of past sinful deeds, through the brilliance of reciting this praise, one attains the state of overcoming all such sinful karma and the births in lower realms; thus, one will not be born in the lower realms. Conversely, it is also taught that one will achieve the perfect attainment of birth in the higher realms; by this, the benefits for both this life and the next within cyclic existence are taught.

The object of the action of praise is the Goddess, that is, the Bhagavatī. The agent is one endowed with genuine reverence. The performer is any intelligent person. As for the manner: it is by being endowed with great faith and diligent effort, and by reciting this praise.

Having risen at dusk and at dawn—that is, having performed the act of rising—and with prostration and offering preceding it, one should keep the qualities of the Āryā in mind. The benefits of this are that she grants all fearlessness; she protects from all fears, such as the eight great fears and the sixteen fears, and she bestows the perfect mastery of the state of fearlessness. Regarding the phrase "recites with diligence" (rab dang brjod cing), since the Sanskrit word "va" is present, it is correct to translate it as "recites with effort." Therefore, if any intelligent person, through the six sessions from dusk onwards, remains reverent toward the Goddess and, by way of remembering her qualities, recites this praise with effort, these benefits will be present; this is how it should be understood throughout the entire preceding and following text.

heading: ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: By reciting the praise to the seventy million Victors and the like, and by remaining in the practice of that, one will swiftly see the faces of the seventy million emanated bodies of the Victors, the Buddhas, who have come and reside together with this Bhagavatī. Having seen them, one will be empowered by them, either in reality or in a dream, through the flowing streams of nectar from their light rays or their hands.

heading: ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།
translation: This also teaches the water empowerment at the time of ripening the student. By the condition of that empowerment, many obscurations are purified, and many distinct meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs are attained, such that one gradually attains the siddhi of Mahāmudrā, which possesses many qualities far greater than this perfect assembly. Having attained that, one traverses the stages of the Āryas and ultimately proceeds to the rank of a perfect, complete Buddha. Thus, the benefits of attaining liberation and omniscience are taught.

"Sin" refers to the fruits of sin; all previously existing illnesses, malevolent spirits, misfortunes, and unfortunate destinies are thoroughly pacified, and those that would have arisen again are averted. Likewise, even if one is a person whose karma makes birth in the lower realms certain due to the power of past sinful deeds, through the brilliance of reciting this praise, one attains the state of overcoming all such sinful karma and the births in lower realms; thus, one will not be born in the lower realms. Conversely, it is also taught that one will achieve the perfect attainment of birth in the higher realms; by this, the benefits for both this life and the next within cyclic existence are taught.

heading: ཕན་ཡོན་བསྟན་པ།
source: དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་དུག་ནི་དག་པོ་ཆེན་པོ་སྟེ། སྲོག་འཕྲོག་པ་དང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཚབས་ཆེན་བསྐྱེད་པའོ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུའི་དུག་དེ་ཡང་སྒྲོལ་མའི་རིག་སྔགས་དྲན་པ་ཙམ་གྱིས། རབ་ཏུ་འཇིགས་པ་སྟེ་དེའི་གནོད་པ་རྣམས་སེལ་ཞིང་། བདུད་རྩིའི་ལ་སོགས་པར་འགྱུར་བའོ། །ཟོས་པ་དང་ནི་འཐུངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་ཞེས་པ་ལྟར་ན། དྲན་པས་རབ་ཏུ་སེལ་ཞེས་པའི་སྔ་རོལ་དུ་སྦྱར་ཏེ། དུག་དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཟོས་པ་དང་འཐུངས་པ་ཉིད་ཀྱང་། རེག་པ་དུག་ཅན་གྱི་བྱུགས་པ་སོགས་ཀྱང་རིག་སྔགས་དྲན་པས་སྐད་ཅིག་ལ་སེལ་ཞེས་པའི་དོན་ཡིན་ལ། འགྱུར་གཞན་ལས་ཟོས་པ་དང་ནི་ཞེས་པ་འདི། དྲན་པས་ཞེས་པའི་ཚིག་གི་འོག་ཏུ་འདོན་པ་ལྟར་ན། ཤྭ་ལོ་ཀ་འོག་མ་དང་སྦྲེལ་བར་འགྲོ་མོད། འོན་ཀྱང་ཁ་དི་ཏཾ་པི་ཏ་མེ་ཝ་པ་ཅེས་འབྱུང་བ་ལྟར་ན། དཀྱུས་ཉིད་བདེའོ། །
translation: Such poison is extremely violent, taking life and causing great suffering. That very poison, by merely remembering the vidyā-mantra of Tārā, is completely terrified—that is, its harms are cleared away and it becomes like nectar. Regarding the phrase "even if eaten or drunk," it should be connected before the phrase "completely eliminated through recollection," meaning that even if such poison has been eaten or drunk, or if one has been touched by poisonous ointments and the like, it is eliminated in an instant by remembering the vidyā-mantra. Although in other translations the phrase "eaten or drunk" is placed after the word "recollection," which would lead to it being connected with the following verse, nevertheless, as it appears as *khāditaṃ pītam eva ca*, the original sequence is correct.

[3-10] translation already produced for this document:
Regarding the "Praise to the Exalted Tārā," the statement that it was spoken by the perfectly complete Buddha Vairocana means that it originates from the *Tārā-mūla-kalpa-nāma-aṣṭaśataka* (The Seven-Hundred-Chapter King of Tantras of Tārā). This is what is asserted. Although the text known as the *Tantra of Various Rites*—which is currently found in this region—also appears, it is the consensus of scholars that it is a composed tantra, and since that position is correct, it does not originate from there. It is not contradictory, however, for it to be a fragment of an extensive tantra or a condensed tantra and so forth. "Completed" (*rdzogs so*) means *samāpta*, which is to say, perfectly attained.
